blogs.title: Beyond the Right-to-Control Theory: How *Constantinescu* Reaffirms Fraud Liability After *Ciminelli*
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory rejected in *Klein v. United States* (*Ciminelli*) and the 'fraudulent inducement' theory upheld in *United States v. Constantinescu*. It explores why the court found that inducing victims to purchase securities constitutes a deprivation of traditional property (money), whereas withholding information regarding asset management does not. The analysis will examine how this ruling preserves the scope of federal fraud statutes in the digital age, ensuring that social media 'pump-and-dump' schemes remain prosecutable despite recent Supreme Court limitations on intangible rights.

blogs.title: Profit Without Loss? The Enduring Validity of the Fraudulent-Inducement Theory Post-*Kousisis*
blogs.description: Focusing on the 'intent to defraud' element, this blog post dissects the defendants' argument that securities fraud requires proof that the victim suffered a net economic loss. Drawing heavily on *Kousisis*, the author argues that *Constantinescu* clarifies that obtaining money or property via deception satisfies statutory requirements even if the victim receives fair-market value for their transaction. The piece discusses how this interpretation dismantles the notion that a 'win-win' scam (where both parties walk away with assets) escapes liability, emphasizing that the core harm lies in the deceptive acquisition of funds rather than subsequent market performance.
